subtopic: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Equations
stem:
Solve the following equations by using determinant
\(\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{y}+\dfrac{1}{z} = -2,\quad \dfrac{1}{x}-\dfrac{2}{y}+\dfrac{1}{z} = 3,\quad \dfrac{2}{x}-\dfrac{1}{y}+\dfrac{3}{2} = -1\)
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the stem's third equation prints \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) where the book's own solution requires \(\dfrac{3}{z}\) (it forms \(2p - q + 3r = -1\)), and a solution line prints \(q = \dfrac{D_q}{q}\) for \(\dfrac{D_q}{D}\). The final answer is unaffected.]

Put \(\dfrac{1}{x} = p,\; \dfrac{1}{y} = q,\; \dfrac{1}{z} = r\)

\(\therefore\) Equations are
\(p + q + r = -2\)
\(p - 2q + r = 3\)
\(2p - q + 3r = -1\)

\(D = \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & -2 & 1\\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 1(-6+1) - 1(3-2) + 1(-1+4)\)
\(= -5 - 1 + 3\)
\(= -3\)

\(Dp = \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1\\ 3 & -2 & 1\\ -1 & -1 & 3\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= -2(-6+1) - 1(9+1) + 1(-3-2)\)
\(= 10 - 10 - 5\)
\(= -5\)

\(Dq = \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & 1\\ 1 & 3 & 1\\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 1(9+1) + 2(3-2) + 1(-1-6)\)
\(= 10 + 2 - 7\)
\(= 5\)

\(Dr = \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & -2\\ 1 & -2 & 3\\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 1(2+3) - 1(-1-6) - 2(-1+4)\)
\(= 5 + 7 - 6\)
\(= 6\)

\(\therefore p = \dfrac{Dp}{D} = \dfrac{-5}{-3} = \dfrac{5}{3},\quad q = \dfrac{Dq}{q} = \dfrac{5}{-3} = \dfrac{-5}{3},\quad r = \dfrac{Dr}{D} = \dfrac{6}{-3} = -2\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{x} = p = \dfrac{5}{3}\;\therefore x = \dfrac{3}{5}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{y} = q = \dfrac{-5}{3}\;\therefore y = \dfrac{-3}{5}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{z} = r = -2\;\therefore z = \dfrac{-1}{2}\)

\(\therefore x = \dfrac{3}{5},\; y = \dfrac{-3}{5},\; z = \dfrac{-1}{2}\) are the solutions of the equations.
_note: TWO printed defects transcribed as they appear. (1) STEM: the third equation is printed as \(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{1}{y}+\frac{3}{2}=-1\); the book's own solution converts it to \(2p-q+3r=-1\), which requires \(\frac{3}{z}\), so the printed '3/2' is a misprint for '3/z'. (2) SOLUTION: the line for q is printed 'q = Dq/q' — the denominator should be D, not q (the numeric value 5/(-3) that follows is correct).

subtopic: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Equations
stem: The cost of 2 books, 6 notebooks and 3 pens is Rs.120. The cost of 3 books, 4 notebooks and 2 pens is Rs.105, while the cost of 5 books, 7 notebooks and 4 pens is Rs.183. Using this information find the cost of 1 book, 1 notebook and 1 pen.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: in the \(D_y\) and \(D_z\) lines the common factor 3 is printed on the left-hand determinant instead of the right. The arithmetic that follows uses the correct placement, so the answer is unaffected.]

Let Rs. \(x\), Rs. \(y\) and Rs. \(z\) be the cost of one book, one notebook and one pen respectively. Then by given information we have,

\(2x + 6y + 3z = 120\)
\(3x + 4y + 2z = 105\)
\(5x + 7y + 4z = 183\)

\(D = \begin{vmatrix}2 & 6 & 3\\ 3 & 4 & 2\\ 5 & 7 & 4\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 2(16-14) - 6(12-10) + 3(21-20)\)
\(= 2(2) - 6(2) + 3(1)\)
\(= 4 - 12 + 3\)
\(= 7 - 12\)
\(= -5\)

\(Dx = \begin{vmatrix}120 & 6 & 3\\ 105 & 4 & 2\\ 183 & 7 & 4\end{vmatrix} = 3\begin{vmatrix}40 & 6 & 3\\ 35 & 4 & 2\\ 61 & 7 & 4\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 3[40(16-14) - 6(140-122) + 3(245-244)]\)
\(= 3[40(2) - 6(18) + 3(1)]\)
\(= 3[80 - 108 + 3]\)
\(= 3[83 - 108]\)
\(= 3[-25] = -75\)

\(Dy = 3\begin{vmatrix}2 & 120 & 3\\ 3 & 105 & 2\\ 5 & 183 & 4\end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix}2 & 40 & 3\\ 3 & 35 & 2\\ 5 & 61 & 4\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 3[2(140-122) - 40(12-10) + 3(183-175)]\)
\(= 3[2(18) - 40(2) + 3(8)]\)
\(= 3[36 - 80 + 24]\)
\(= 3[60 - 80]\)
\(= 3[-20]\)
\(= -60\)

\(Dz = 3\begin{vmatrix}2 & 6 & 40\\ 3 & 4 & 35\\ 5 & 7 & 61\end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix}2 & 6 & 120\\ 3 & 4 & 105\\ 5 & 7 & 183\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 3[2(244-245) - 6(183-175) + 40(21-20)]\)
\(= 3[2(-1) - 6(8) + 40(1)]\)
\(= 3[-2 - 48 + 40]\)
\(= 3[-50 + 40]\)
\(= 3[-10]\)
\(= -30\)

\(\therefore x = \dfrac{Dx}{D} = \dfrac{-75}{-5} = 15,\quad y = \dfrac{Dy}{D} = \dfrac{-60}{-5} = 12,\quad z = \dfrac{Dz}{D} = \dfrac{-30}{-5} = 6\)

\(\therefore\) Rs.15, Rs. 12, Rs. 6 are the costs of one book, one notebook and one pen respectively.
_note: Printed defect transcribed as it appears: in the \(Dy\) and \(Dz\) lines the common factor 3 is printed on the LEFT determinant instead of the right, i.e. the book prints '\(Dy = 3|2\;120\;3;\ldots| = |2\;40\;3;\ldots|\)' where it should read '\(Dy = |2\;120\;3;\ldots| = 3|2\;40\;3;\ldots|\)' (and likewise for \(Dz\)). The arithmetic that follows uses the correct placement, so the final answers are right.

subtopic: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Equations
stem:
Verify the consistency of following equations
\(2x+2y = -2,\quad x + y = -1,\quad 3x + 3y = -5\)
solution:
By condition of consistency consider

\(\begin{vmatrix}a_1 & b_1 & c_1\\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2\\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3\end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 & 2\\ 1 & 1 & 1\\ 3 & 3 & 5\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 2(5-3) - 2(5-3) + 2(3-3) = 4 - 4 + 0 = 0\)

But the equations have no common Solution. Equations are not consistent.

subtopic: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Equations
context: Examine the consistency of following equations.
solution:
Write the given equation in standard form.

\(x + y - 2 = 0,\quad 2x + 3y - 5 = 0,\quad 3x - 2y - 1 = 0\)

Solving first two equations, we get \(x = 1,\; y = 1\).

And \((1,1)\) satisfy the third equation.

\(\therefore\) Given equations have a common solution.

\(\therefore\) Given system of equations is consistent.

subtopic: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Equations
context: Examine the consistency of following equations.
solution:
\(x + y = 1,\; 2x + 2y = 2,\; 3x + 3y = 5\) are given equations.

Check the condition of consistency.

\(\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & -1\\ 2 & 2 & -2\\ 3 & 3 & -5\end{vmatrix} = 2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & -1\\ 1 & 1 & -1\\ 3 & 3 & -5\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 2(0) = 0\)  (\(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are identical)

Let us examine further.

Note that lines given by the equations \(x + y = 1\) and \(3x + 3y = 5\) are parallel to each other. They do not have a common solution, so equations are not consistent.

subtopic: Cramer's Rule and Consistency of Equations
stem:
Find the value of k if the following equations are consistent.
\(7x - ky = 4,\quad 2x + 5y = 9\) and \(2x + y = 8\)
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the top-right entry of the printed determinant is set as \(4\). Since the first equation in standard form is \(7x - ky - 4 = 0\), that entry is \(-4\), and the book's own expansion does use \(-4\) (it reaches \(-217 + 2k + 32 = 0\)). The printed answer \(k = \dfrac{185}{2}\) is CORRECT — confirmed independently of the determinant: the two \(k\)-free lines meet at \(\left(\dfrac{31}{8},\ \dfrac{1}{4}\right)\), and the third line passes through that point exactly when \(k = \dfrac{185}{2}\).]

Given equations
\(7x - ky - 4 = 0,\quad 2x + 5y - 9 = 0,\quad 2x + y - 8 = 0\) are consistent

\(\therefore \begin{vmatrix}7 & -k & 4\\ 2 & 5 & -9\\ 2 & 1 & -8\end{vmatrix} = 0\)

\(\therefore 7(-40+9) + k(-16+18) - 4(2-10) = 0\)
\(\therefore 7(-31) + 2k - 4(-8) = 0\)
\(\therefore -217 + 2k + 32 = 0\;\Rightarrow\; -185 + 2k = 0\)
\(\therefore 2k = 185\quad \therefore k = \dfrac{185}{2}\)
_note: Printed defect transcribed as it appears. Two problems: (a) the stem writes the first determinant entry as \(4\) after moving \(-4\) to the left side (the standard form is \(7x-ky-4=0\), so the third column entry should be \(-4\)); (b) the third cofactor term is printed with a MINUS sign, '\(-4(2-10)\)', but expanding along row 1 gives \(+a_{13}M_{13} = +4(2-10) = -32\). With the correct sign the equation is \(-217 + 2k - 32 = 0\), giving \(2k = 249\) and \(k = \frac{249}{2}\), not the printed \(\frac{185}{2}\). Transcribed as printed; a cross-check pass should adjudicate.

subtopic: Area of a Triangle and Collinearity
stem: Find the area of the triangle whose vertices are A\((-2, -3)\), B\((3, 2)\) and C\((-1, -8)\).
solution:
Given \((x_1, y_1) = (-2, -3)\), \((x_2, y_2) = (3, 2)\), and \((x_3, y_3) = (-1, -8)\)

We know that area of triangle
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix}x_1 & y_1 & 1\\ x_2 & y_2 & 1\\ x_3 & y_3 & 1\end{vmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -3 & 1\\ 3 & 2 & 1\\ -1 & -8 & 1\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}[-2(2+8) + 3(3+1) + 1(-24+2)]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}[-20 + 12 - 22]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}[-42 + 12] = \dfrac{1}{2}[-30] = -15\)

Area is positive.

\(\therefore\) Area of triangle = 15 square unit

This gives the area of the triangle ABC in that order of the vertices. If we consider the same triangle as ACB, then triangle is considered in opposite orientation. The area then is 15 sq. units. This also agrees with the rule that interchanging 2nd and 3rd rows changes the sign of the determinant.

subtopic: Area of a Triangle and Collinearity
stem: If the area of triangle with vertices P\((-3, 0)\), Q\((3, 0)\) and R\((0, K)\) is 9 square unit then find the value of k.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed working shows \(\pm 9 = \dfrac{1}{2}[3 + 3k]\); both cofactor terms are \(3k\), so the bracket is \(6k\). The next line \(\pm 9 = 3k\) and the answer \(k = \pm 3\) are correct.]

Given \((x_1, y_1) \equiv (-3, 0)\), \((x_2, y_2) \equiv (3, 0)\) and \((x_3, y_3) \equiv (0, k)\) and area of \(\Delta\) is 9 sq. unit.

We know that area of \(\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix}x_1 & y_1 & 1\\ x_2 & y_2 & 1\\ x_3 & y_3 & 1\end{vmatrix}\)

\(\therefore \pm 9 = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 & 1\\ 3 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & k & 1\end{vmatrix}\)  (Area is positive but the determinant can be of either sign)

\(\therefore \pm 9 = \dfrac{1}{2}[-3(0-k) + 1(3k-0)]\)

\(\therefore \pm 9 = \dfrac{1}{2}[3 + 3k]\quad \therefore \pm 9 = 3k \quad \therefore k = \pm 3\)
_note: Printed defect transcribed as it appears: the line '\(\pm 9 = \frac{1}{2}[3 + 3k]\)' should read '\(\frac{1}{2}[3k + 3k]\)' — both cofactor terms evaluate to \(3k\), so the bracket is \(6k\). The next line '\(\pm 9 = 3k\)' and the answer \(k = \pm 3\) follow from the correct \(6k\), so only the printed bracket is wrong. Also note the stem prints the vertex as R(0, K) with a capital K while the solution uses lower-case k.

subtopic: Area of a Triangle and Collinearity
stem: Find the area of triangle whose vertices are A\((3, 7)\), B\((4, -3)\) and C\((5, -13)\). Interpret your answer.
solution:
Given \((x_1, y_1) \equiv (3, 7)\), \((x_2, y_2) \equiv (4, -3)\) and \((x_3, y_3) \equiv (5, -13)\)

Area of \(\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix}x_1 & y_1 & 1\\ x_2 & y_2 & 1\\ x_3 & y_3 & 1\end{vmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 7 & 1\\ 4 & -3 & 1\\ 5 & -13 & 1\end{vmatrix}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}[3(-3+13) - 7(4-5) + 1(-52+15)]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}[30 + 7 - 37] = \dfrac{1}{2}[37-37] = 0\)

\(A(\Delta ABC) = 0\quad \therefore\) A, B, C are collinear points

subtopic: Area of a Triangle and Collinearity
stem:
Show that the following points are collinear by determinant method.
A\((2, 5)\), B\((5, 7)\), C\((8, 9)\)
solution:
Given \(A \equiv (x_1, y_1) = (2, 5)\), \(B \equiv (x_2, y_2) \equiv (5, 7)\), \(C \equiv (x_3, y_3) \equiv (8, 9)\)

If \(\begin{vmatrix}x_1 & y_1 & 1\\ x_2 & y_2 & 1\\ x_3 & y_3 & 1\end{vmatrix} = 0\) then, A, B, C are collinear

\(\therefore \begin{vmatrix}2 & 5 & 1\\ 5 & 7 & 1\\ 8 & 9 & 1\end{vmatrix} = 2(7-9) - 5(5-8) + 1(45-56)\)
\(= -4 + 15 - 11\quad = -15 + 15 = 0\)

\(\therefore\) A, B, C are collinear.
